 Drought during the rainy season
 In mid-November, many provinces in central Vietnam experienced unusual weather patterns.
 Báo Sài Gòn Giải phóng • 18/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 In mid-November, many provinces in central Vietnam experienced unusual weather patterns. Instead of the usual torrential rains and warnings of flash floods and landslides that have become a harsh reality every late autumn and early winter, the area was scorching hot. This anomaly caused concern among those involved in water resource management and control.
 On November 17th, the Da Nang City People's Committee issued Official Document No. 12159/UBND-KT, agreeing to allow two large hydropower reservoirs, Song Tranh 2 and Dak Mi 4A, located upstream of the Vu Gia - Thu Bon river basin, to proactively store water to cope with the risk of drought and water shortage in 2027 due to the impact of El Niño.
 Thus, instead of straining themselves to combat floods as in previous years, local authorities are now having to carefully plan to "conserve every drop of water" for the upcoming dry season. In fact, the situation in the Vu Gia - Thu Bon river basin in recent days shows that this concern is entirely justified.
 Although the rainy season is almost over, rainfall across the entire basin is severely deficient compared to the multi-year average. Upstream reservoirs are facing water shortages. Many large cascaded hydropower reservoirs in the basin have yet to reach their normal water levels – the minimum safe threshold to ensure water supply for domestic use, agricultural production, and salinity control in downstream areas for the next 8-9 months of the dry season.
 The disruption of climate patterns is posing a "double" challenge to the operation of interconnected reservoirs. On the one hand, the risk of El Niño extending into 2027 forces hydropower plants and local authorities to take advantage of every last light rain of the season to accumulate water, avoiding a repeat of the severe saltwater intrusion scenario at each river mouth, which left millions of downstream residents without access to clean water, as in previous extreme years.
 On the other hand, the uncertainty of climate change means that floods in Central Vietnam always have the potential for extreme and unpredictable events; late storms or unusually heavy rainfall patterns can strike at any time. Therefore, in the directive issued on November 17th, the leaders of Da Nang City particularly emphasized the "dual" principle: allowing early water storage but strictly adhering to the Inter-Reservoir Operation Procedure according to Decision No. 2138/QD-TTg of the Prime Minister, absolutely avoiding sudden changes in flow, and immediately switching to flood control and reduction mode for downstream areas when unusual rainfall and flooding situations occur.
 The story of "worrying about drought during the rainy season" in Da Nang in 2026 once again shows that the traditional concepts of "rainy season" or "dry season" are gradually being erased by climate change.
 When nature no longer operates according to experience, human initiative, flexibility in management, and scientific planning become the strongest shield to protect the safety and sustainable livelihoods of downstream areas.
